name: Tree Jumps
description: You are given a rooted tree, consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices. The vertices in the tree are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, and the root is the vertex $$$1$$$. Let $$$d_x$$$ be the distance (the number of edges on the shortest path) from the root to the vertex $$$x$$$. There is a chip that is initially placed at the root. You can perform the following operation as many times as you want (possibly zero): move the chip from the current vertex $$$v$$$ to a vertex $$$u$$$ such that $$$d_u = d_v + 1$$$. If $$$v$$$ is the root, you can choose any vertex $$$u$$$ meeting this constraint; however, if $$$v$$$ is not the root, $$$u$$$ should not be a neighbor of $$$v$$$ (there should be no edge connecting $$$v$$$ and $$$u$$$). For example, in the tree above, the following chip moves are possible: $$$1 \rightarrow 2$$$, $$$1 \rightarrow 5$$$, $$$2 \rightarrow 7$$$, $$$5 \rightarrow 3$$$, $$$5 \rightarrow 4$$$, $$$3 \rightarrow 6$$$, $$$7 \rightarrow 6$$$. A sequence of vertices is valid if you can move the chip in such a way that it visits all vertices from the sequence (and only them), in the order they are given in the sequence. Your task is to calculate the number of valid vertex sequences. Since the answer might be large, print it modulo $$$998244353$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$). The second line contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$p_2, p_3, \dots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \lt i$$$), where $$$p_i$$$ is the parent of the $$$i$$$-th vertex in the tree. Vertex $$$1$$$ is the root. Additional constraint on the input: the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $$$3 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the number of valid vertex sequences, taken modulo $$$998244353$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2070D — Tree Jumps [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
